items: Identify the Regression Type: Observe whether your child has occasional accidents without strong emotions, frequent accidents when you're busy with the baby, or genuine distress and withholding behaviors.
Identify the Regression Type: Track when accidents happen most often to determine if they correlate with divided attention, which indicates an attention-seeking regression.
Identify the Regression Type: Watch for anxiety signals like new clinginess, sleep disruption, baby talk, or regression in other areas, which signal an anxiety-driven regression.
Identify the Regression Type: Check for physical symptoms like straining, hard stools, blood in stool, crying during bowel movements, or frequent urination, which require medical attention.
Respond Based on Type: If your child has a normal developmental regression, clean up accidents neutrally without drama, punishment, or excessive praise and simply move on.
Respond Based on Type: If your child is seeking attention through accidents, give a brief calm response like 'You had an accident, let's clean it up' with no long conversations.
Respond Based on Type: For attention-seeking regressions, schedule at least 10 minutes of completely uninterrupted one-on-one time with your older child every single day.
Respond Based on Type: For anxiety-driven regressions, prioritize connection and physical comfort over potty training pressure and help your child's nervous system settle first.
Know When to Get Help: Contact your pediatrician if your child shows signs of constipation or withholding, since chronic constipation makes regression significantly harder to resolve.
Know When to Get Help: Seek medical evaluation immediately if you notice straining, blood in stool, crying during bowel movements, or symptoms of a urinary tract infection.
Know When to Get Help: Give the regression time to resolve using the appropriate response method, since most regressions pass within 2 to 12 weeks when handled correctly.
Know When to Get Help: Trust that this regression is temporary and almost always resolves, so focus on low-pressure response rather than forcing quick results.
